transcript:
HEADER:
Date: 2026-10-13
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~53 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (WillowRun Head of Platform), Tom Brooks (WillowRun Network Ops), Sana Iqbal (WillowRun Security), Evan Lee (SRE), Lena Park (PM)

SUMMARY:
Quick kickoff for private/VPC onramp. Primary goals: verify network constraints (peering, transit gateway, egress), align on region gating & data residency, confirm stakeholders for SOC2/KMS/SSO review, and agree next technical deep-dive and artifacts to exchange.

TOPICS COVERED:
- VPC peering vs PrivateLink/private endpoints vs Transit Gateway
- Egress IP management and NAT/egress requirements
- Region availability and data residency (EU/US split)
- Compliance needs: SOC2, KMS integration, audit logs, SSO/SAML
- Pilot sizing and timeline (small pilot -> dedicated pool/Private)

NOTES / LINKS REFERENCED:
- redwood-private-checklist.pdf (Redwood shared doc)
- networking-playbook.xlsx (customer requested)
- security-compliance.pdf (Redwood SOC2 artifacts)

TRANSCRIPT:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. Diego, our solutions engineer, is here to run through networking and any nitty gritty details.
[00:12] Aisha Patel: Hi all, Aisha here. We run WillowRun's inference platform and we're evaluating Redwood for private deployment. Main constraints: we need EU residency for a subset of data, and we have a transit gateway‑forwarding architecture.
[00:26] Diego Ramos: Great, thanks Aisha. Maybe I can start by outlining the typical private deployment patterns we see — there's VPC peering, private endpoints / privatelink, and transit gateway peering — each has pros and cons.
[00:38] Tom Brooks: Quick interjection — we prefer not to peer our production VPCs directly with vendor VPCs; we'd rather use transit gateway or PrivateLink because of routing controls.
[00:52] Diego Ramos: Totally — transit gateway is common at the enterprise scale. We often use PrivateLink for per‑region private endpoints if customers want strict people‑to‑vendor isolation and no cross‑account route leakage.
[01:05] Lena Park: Is there a latency tradeoff between PrivateLink and peering? We have low latency requirements for inference (p95 < 120ms) in EU region for one of our product flows.
[01:18] Diego Ramos: PrivateLink adds a hop but it's usually consistent; most customers see single‑digit ms add. If you need micro‑latency we recommend colocated model variants in the same AZ/region and reserved capacity. Also we'll want to understand payload sizes — batching helps.
[01:33] Evan Lee: On the data residency piece — can Redwood host two separate private deployments (one EU, one US) and route calls from our EU app to EU-only infra?
[01:43] Maya Chen: Yes — customers can pin model versions to a region. Redwood Private supports region gating; we can run separate control planes if needed, or use VPCs in the EU region for strict residency.
[01:55] Sana Iqbal: For security, we need to understand KMS integration — do you allow customer‑managed keys (CMKs) and HSM integrations? Also audit logs and retention.
[02:07] Diego Ramos: We support KMS integrations in Private — customer managed keys are possible; HSM depends on the deployment tier. We'll send the KMS integration playbook. Audit logs are available via console exports or S3 delivery for private deployments.
[02:22] Tom Brooks: Egress: we need predictable IPs for allowlisting. How does Redwood handle outbound calls from the hosted runtime to our services?
[02:30] Diego Ramos: For Private deployments, you get configured egress IPs — either static NAT gateways we provision in your account or we can route through your NAT with peered private connection. We also offer an egress proxy layer for allowlisting.
[02:45] Tom Brooks: Right, because our external models call home for some telemetry and we need allowlisting. Also do you support SNAT/elastic IP mapping so we can tie security groups and WAF rules?
[02:56] Diego Ramos: Yes, elastic IPs are possible; we can discuss whether to use a centralized NAT or per‑subnet NAT depending on your scale.
[03:07] Aisha Patel: Timeline — we're aiming for a pilot in November, with production in Jan if all good. We'll need a short security review and maybe a perf benchmark.
[03:18] Maya Chen: Sounds reasonable. For the pilot we typically spin up a small private pool — we can present a couple of options: hosted private lanes vs reserved dedicated pool. We'll include perf runbook and a benchmark spreadsheet.
[03:30] Lena Park: Who would own the initial network config? We can throw over our TGW attachments and route tables if you share a checklist.
[03:38] Maya Chen: We'll share a private deployment checklist — it lists required TGW IDs, subnet CIDRs, route table changes, security groups, and the IP ranges you should allowlist.
[03:49] Tom Brooks: Do you support cross‑account PrivateLink endpoints or do we need to create endpoint services in our account?
[03:56] Diego Ramos: We create endpoint services on our side and you create the interface endpoints in your VPC. For PrivateLink, cross‑account is standard; we publish the service name and you accept the endpoint. For transit gateway we can peer to your TGW via attachments.
[04:10] Evan Lee: Any caveats with IPv6? We're starting to test dual stack in some regions.
[04:16] Diego Ramos: Our runtime supports IPv4 primarily; IPv6 support is on the roadmap — we'll note that as a constraint for your EU pilot.
[04:25] Sana Iqbal: Compliance checklist: besides SOC2, we need encryption‑at‑rest using customer KMS, SSO via SAML/Okta, RBAC, and audit logs with 12‑month retention.
[04:38] Maya Chen: Understood — our Private offering hits most of those. We'll attach SOC2 artifacts and a SAML integration guide. For RBAC we support scoped roles and token issuance controls.
[04:50] Aisha Patel: Cost question — for dedicated reserved pool vs hosted private — what's the ballpark? We need order‑of‑magnitude for finance to budget.
[04:59] Maya Chen: I'll follow up with a detailed quote, but high level: reserved dedicated pools are higher up‑front but lower per‑token cost and guaranteed capacity. Hosted private (shared hardware within a VPC-like private tenancy) is cheaper initially and faster to onboard. I'll send two pricing scenarios.
[05:14] Tom Brooks: Network sizing — what's the expected throughput per VM? We need to know expected burst bandwidth and whether you require jumbo MTU for perf.
[05:23] Diego Ramos: Throughput depends on model and sequence lengths. We'll request sample traffic profile — typical LLM traffic is small packets but high token rates; we don't require jumbo MTU for most customers but if you do heavy binary transfers we can accommodate. We'll include sample perf numbers for the model families you mentioned.
[05:40] Lena Park: Does Redwood run any egress DNS or service discovery that requires us to open specific ports?
[05:46] Diego Ramos: We use outbound HTTPS to our control plane and artifact stores; we'll provide the exact FQDNs and IP ranges. For Private deployments most control plane calls can be routed over private connectivity so you might not need public egress, depending on the topology.
[06:02] Tom Brooks: Any gotchas for transit gateway routing propagation? We prefer explicit route table entries rather than broad route propagation.
[06:10] Diego Ramos: We can work with explicit routes. For TGW we usually set up specific attachments and control route propagation per attachment for security.
[06:20] Aisha Patel: Do you support bringing your own VPC vs Redwood provisioning subnets in our account?
[06:27] Maya Chen: Both patterns work — many customers prefer vendor-managed subnets to simplify setup, but if you need control we can deploy in your account via CloudFormation / Terraform templates.
[06:38] Sana Iqbal: For the KMS flow — are encryption keys accessible to Redwood engineers? We need assurance keys stay under our KMS policy.
[06:46] Diego Ramos: In Private deployments, keys remain in your KMS; Redwood doesn't export raw key material. We can define IAM roles and key policies to restrict access. We'll share the KMS integration guide.
[06:58] Evan Lee: On monitoring: can we forward Audit logs and per‑route latency metrics into our prometheus or datadog?
[07:05] Diego Ramos: Yes, logs can be exported to S3 or pushed into your logging/metrics system via a forwarder. We have a Datadog integration and sample dashboards.
[07:16] Lena Park: Regarding region gating — if we have one tenant in EU and one in US, can we have a single control plane for both or do you prefer separate control planes for strict compliance?
[07:28] Maya Chen: We can do either. For strict compliance we often stand up a regional control plane to ensure metadata and logs remain in‑region. We'll discuss options in the follow up.
[07:39] Aisha Patel: For the pilot we'll aim to test a small NLU model first, not the largest 70B ones — want to validate latency and cost first.
[07:48] Diego Ramos: Perfect — that gives us a sensible baseline. We'll propose a pilot config and a small perf run.
[07:55] Tom Brooks: One more network detail: do you support VPC DNS resolution across PrivateLink endpoints? We rely on internal hostnames.
[08:02] Diego Ramos: Yes, we provide guidance to set up private hosted zones and conditional forwarding if needed. There are a few steps for cross‑account DNS for PrivateLink but it's doable.
[08:12] Maya Chen: Ok, let's capture next steps — I'll send the checklist, the pricing scenarios, SOC2 artifacts, and a sample network diagram. Diego will schedule the deep technical session with Tom and Evan for next week.
[08:24] Aisha Patel: Sounds good, thanks.
[08:27] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone.
[08:30] [call ends]
